```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%",
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.2, comment = "##")
options(width = 90)
```

This tutorial shows how to use **DenMark** to quantify the correlation between
gene expression and cell density in single-cell resolution spatial
transcriptomics (ST) data, and how to identify the density-correlated genes
(DCGs). All analyses use the user-level functions in `DenMark-functions.R`
together with the two Stan models:

* `DenMark-M2.stan`: the full DenMark model, with dependent density and expression latent fields;
* `DenMark-M1.stan`: the simplified DenMark model, with independent fields and $a_{21}=0$, used for model comparison.

Each model also has a variable-area version, `DenMark-M2-vararea.stan` and
`DenMark-M1-vararea.stan`. These are identical except that every grid cell has
its own area offset. They are used automatically when the analysis is
restricted to the tissue by an alpha-shape boundary, as in this tutorial.

For a grid cell $g$ with area $|g|$ inside the tissue, cell count $Y(g)$ and
summed expression $M(g)$, the full model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y(g) &\sim \text{Poisson}\{\lambda_1(g)\}, & \log\lambda_1(g) &= \log|g| + \beta_0 + a_{11}w_1(g),\\
M(g)\mid Y(g) &\sim \text{Poisson}\{\lambda_2(g)\}, & \log\lambda_2(g) &= \beta_1 + \log\{Y(g)+0.05\} + a_{21}w_1(g) + a_{22}w_2(g),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $w_1, w_2$ are independent unit-variance Matérn-3/2 Gaussian processes,
approximated with Hilbert-space basis functions (HSGP). With
$a_{11}=\sigma_1$, $a_{21}=\sigma_2\rho$ and $a_{22}=\sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$,
the parameter $\rho$, named `Astar[2,1]` in Stan, is the **density-expression
correlation**.

This tutorial runs on a **simulated** dataset in which the true
density-expression correlations are known, so every result can be checked
against the truth. The simulated data have the same structure as real
single-cell resolution ST data, so the same steps apply directly to, for
example, the 10x Xenium human breast cancer dataset
([In Situ Sample 1, Replicate 1](https://www.10xgenomics.com/products/xenium-in-situ/preview-dataset-human-breast)).
A real analysis starts from two files:

* `cell_spatial.csv`: the 2D locations and cell types of the cells, one row per cell ID;
* `cell_by_gene_expression.csv`: the raw gene expression of the cells, one row per cell ID and one column per gene.

Code Block 1.2 shows how to load these two files in place of the simulated data.

Section 1 simulates the data and sets the hyperparameters. Section 2 selects the
region of interest (ROI), delineates the tissue with an alpha shape, filters
the genes and grids the data. Section 3
quantifies the density-expression relationship for one gene. Section 4
identifies the DCGs, and Section 5 shows the same workflow in Python.

> **Running this file.** Put `DenMark-functions.R` and the four Stan files
> `DenMark-M1.stan`, `DenMark-M2.stan`, `DenMark-M1-vararea.stan` and
> `DenMark-M2-vararea.stan` in the folder given by the `denmark_dir` parameter.
> A relative `denmark_dir` such as the default `"DenMark"` is read from the
> folder that contains this Rmd file; an absolute path such as
> `"C:/Users/name/Desktop/Tutorial/DenMark"` also works. If the DenMark files
> sit next to the Rmd file, they are found there as well. Then
> knit, or run `rmarkdown::render("Tutorial_DenMark.Rmd")`. Fitted models are
> saved in `fit_dir` and reused on the next knit. Set `refit: true` to refit.

---

# 0. Prepare packages and functions

DenMark runs Stan through **cmdstanr**, which needs a working CmdStan
installation. Install both once, following <https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/>:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# [Code Block 0.1] One-time installation
install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(cores = 4)

# packages used by the DenMark functions and this tutorial
install.packages(c("posterior", "loo", "ggplot2", "patchwork", "knitr", "sf"))
```

Load the packages and the DenMark functions. `rstan` and `rethinking` are no
longer needed.

```{r load}
# [Code Block 0.2] Load packages and DenMark functions
library(cmdstanr)
library(posterior)
library(loo)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)

if (nzchar(params$cmdstan_path)) set_cmdstan_path(params$cmdstan_path)
cmdstan_version()

# Locate the DenMark folder. Relative paths are read from the folder that
# contains this Rmd file, which is the working directory when knitting.
# The folder given by `denmark_dir` is tried first, then the Rmd folder itself.
denmark_files <- c("DenMark-functions.R", "DenMark-M1.stan", "DenMark-M2.stan",
                   "DenMark-M1-vararea.stan", "DenMark-M2-vararea.stan")
candidates <- unique(c(params$denmark_dir, "."))
found <- candidates[file.exists(file.path(candidates, "DenMark-functions.R"))]
if (length(found) == 0)
  stop("DenMark-functions.R was not found in: ",
       paste(normalizePath(candidates, mustWork = FALSE), collapse = " or "),
       ". Set `denmark_dir` in the YAML header to the folder with the DenMark files.")
denmark_dir <- normalizePath(found[1])
missing <- denmark_files[!file.exists(file.path(denmark_dir, denmark_files))]
if (length(missing) > 0)
  stop("Missing in ", denmark_dir, ": ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
if (!requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE))
  stop("The tissue boundary needs the 'sf' package: install.packages('sf')")
denmark_dir

# DenMark functions; the Stan files are looked up in the same folder
source(file.path(denmark_dir, "DenMark-functions.R"))
options(denmark.stan_dir = denmark_dir)

# folder for the saved fits, created if it does not exist
fit_dir <- params$fit_dir
dir.create(fit_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# a compact table printer for this document
show_table <- function(x, digits = 3, ...) {
  kable(x, digits = digits, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, ...)
}
```

The functions used in this tutorial are:

| Step | Function | Purpose |
|:-----|:---------|:--------|
| QC | `denmark_filter_genes()` | keep informative genes |
| Tissue boundary | `denmark_alpha_shape()` | alpha shape of all cells in the section |
| Gridding | `buildgridpp()`, `grid_pts_centroid()` | cell counts $Y$, expression $M$, grid geometry |
| Fitting | `DenMark()` | fit M2 (full) or M1 (simplified) to one gene |
| Summaries | `denmark_summary()`, `denmark_draws()`, `denmark_compare()` | posterior summary, $\rho$ draws, WAIC |
| Interpretation | `denmark_fields()`, `denmark_decay()` | latent field decomposition, spatial correlation ranges |
| DCG discovery | `denmark_scan()` | fit many genes, classify PCG / NCG |
| Plots | `plot_denmark_boundary()`, `plot_denmark_grid()`, `plot_denmark_fields()`, `plot_denmark_decay()`, `plot_denmark_scan()` | figures |

# 1. Simulate single-cell resolution ST data and select hyperparameters

We simulate cells from the DenMark data-generating process with
`denmark_simulate()`. As in a real section, the cells lie in an irregular,
lobed piece of tissue inside a 6 mm $\times$ 4 mm window, not in a rectangle.
The tissue holds about 5,000 cells of the analyzed cell type and 4,000 cells
of other types. The analyzed cells carry three genes with known
density-expression correlations: geneA with $\rho = 0.6$, geneB with
$\rho = 0$ and geneC with $\rho = -0.6$. A fourth, rarely detected gene is
added to show the quality-control step.

```{r data-sim}
# [Code Block 1.1] Simulate data with known rho
sim <- denmark_simulate(rho = c(geneA = 0.6, geneB = 0, geneC = -0.6),
                        width = 6, height = 4, n_cells = 5000, seed = 1,
                        tissue = "irregular", n_other = 4000,
                        celltype = params$celltype)
table(sim$celltype)

# arrange the simulated data in the same two tables as a real dataset
cell_spatial <- data.frame(X = seq_len(nrow(sim)) - 1, x = sim$x, y = sim$y,
                           celltype = sim$celltype)
cell_gene <- data.frame(cell_id = cell_spatial$X, sim[, c("geneA", "geneB", "geneC")])
cell_gene$lowGene <- rpois(nrow(sim), 0.01)  # rarely detected, removed by QC below
head(cell_spatial)
head(cell_gene)

gene_choice <- "geneA"
scan_genes  <- c("geneA", "geneB", "geneC")
unit_label  <- "mm"
```

**Using a real dataset.** To analyze the Xenium data instead, run Code Block
1.2 in place of Code Block 1.1. It creates the same objects: `cell_spatial`,
`cell_gene`, `gene_choice`, `scan_genes` and `unit_label`. The rest of the
tutorial is unchanged. In this document the chunk is shown but not run; set
`eval = TRUE` in its header, or run it in the console, to use it. The
`data_dir`, `gene` and `scan_genes` parameters in the YAML header set the
data folder, the gene analyzed in Section 3 and the genes scanned in
Section 4.

```{r data-xenium, eval = FALSE}
# [Code Block 1.2] Optional: load the Xenium breast cancer data
cell_gene    <- read.csv(file.path(params$data_dir, "cell_by_gene_expression.csv"),
                         check.names = FALSE)               # cell ID x genes
cell_spatial <- read.csv(file.path(params$data_dir, "cell_spatial.csv"))
                                                            # cell ID, x, y, celltype
dim(cell_gene)
colnames(cell_gene)[2:6]   # the first 5 genes

# coordinates from micrometers to millimeters
cell_spatial$x <- cell_spatial$x / 1000
cell_spatial$y <- cell_spatial$y / 1000

gene_choice <- params$gene         # e.g. "CDH1"
scan_genes  <- params$scan_genes   # e.g. CDH1, ERBB2, EPCAM, KRT8
unit_label  <- "mm"
```

The hyperparameters control the approximation precision:

* `grid_size`: number of grid cells per axis, given as a single number or as `c(nx, ny)`;
* `basis`: number of HSGP basis functions per axis. More basis functions approximate shorter length-scales better, at a higher computational cost;
* `boundfactor`: HSGP boundary factor $c \ge 1$, which removes boundary effects; $c = 1.5$ is a good default.

```{r hyper}
# [Code Block 1.3] Select hyperparameters
grid_size       <- params$grid_size
basis_choice    <- params$basis
boundary_choice <- params$boundfactor

# sampler settings used for every fit in this tutorial
mcmc <- list(chains = params$chains, iter_warmup = params$iter_warmup,
             iter_sampling = params$iter_sampling, adapt_delta = 0.95,
             max_treedepth = 10, seed = 2024)
c(grid_size = grid_size, basis = basis_choice, boundfactor = boundary_choice)
```

# 2. ROI selection, gene filtering and gridding

The ROI is chosen to suit the research question. Here we run DenMark on all
cells of one cell type across the whole tissue, which is a large-range analysis. A
smaller window can be analyzed the same way by subsetting the cells, or by
passing `bbox = c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)` to the functions.

```{r roi, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Cells of the selected cell type."}
# [Code Block 2.1] Extract the cell type of interest
sel <- which(cell_spatial$celltype == params$celltype)
cells_roi <- cell_spatial[sel, ]
gene_roi  <- cell_gene[sel, -1, drop = FALSE]  # drop the cell ID column
cat(length(sel), "cells of type", params$celltype, "\n")

ggplot(cells_roi, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("x (", unit_label, ")"), y = paste0("y (", unit_label, ")")) +
  theme_classic()

# Short-range analysis: e.g. a pathologist-selected window [0.5, 1.5] * [2, 3]
# keep <- with(cell_spatial, x >= 0.5 & x <= 1.5 & y >= 2 & y <= 3)
```

**Tissue boundary.** A tissue section is not a rectangle. If the grid
covered the whole bounding box, grid cells outside the tissue would contain
no cells simply because there is no tissue there, and the model would read
them as regions of low cell density. We therefore delineate the tissue with an
alpha shape. `denmark_alpha_shape()` triangulates the cell locations and keeps
every Delaunay triangle whose circumradius is below $\alpha$; the union of the
kept triangles is the tissue. By default $\alpha$ is three times the median
Delaunay edge length. The boundary is computed from **all** cells of the
section, not only the analyzed cell type, because the region where a cell type
could have been observed is the whole tissue.

```{r boundary, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Left: all cells, the analyzed cell type in red, and the alpha-shape tissue boundary. Right: grid cells classified as interior, boundary or exterior."}
# [Code Block 2.2] Tissue boundary by alpha shape, computed from all cells
tissue <- denmark_alpha_shape(cell_spatial$x, cell_spatial$y)
c(alpha = attr(tissue, "alpha"), tissue_area = as.numeric(sf::st_area(tissue)))

# grid over the tissue: each grid cell gets its area inside the tissue and a type
grid_types <- buildgridpp(grid_size = grid_size,
                          dataset = data.frame(cells_roi[, c("x", "y")], n = 1),
                          boundary = tissue)
table(grid_types$grid$type)

plot_denmark_boundary(cell_spatial, tissue, grid = grid_types,
                      highlight = cell_spatial$celltype == params$celltype,
                      xlab = unit_label, ylab = unit_label)
```

Each grid cell is classified as **interior**, entirely inside the tissue,
**boundary**, partly inside, or **exterior**, outside the tissue. Exterior grid
cells are removed. Boundary grid cells are kept with their clipped area
$|g \cap \text{tissue}|$, so the area offset $\log|g|$ in the model becomes
a per-grid vector, and `DenMark()` switches to the variable-area Stan models.
All of this happens when `boundary = tissue` is passed to the DenMark
functions below. Without a `boundary`, the whole bounding box is used with a
common grid area, as in the original DenMark analysis.

**Quality control.** Genes in the lowest 5% of variance across cells, or
detected in fewer than 5% of the cells, are removed.

```{r qc}
# [Code Block 2.3] Filter uninformative genes
genes_keep <- denmark_filter_genes(gene_roi, var_quantile = 0.05, min_nonzero = 0.05)
length(genes_keep)
head(genes_keep, 10)

# combined data set for DenMark: one row per cell, columns x, y, genes
final_df <- data.frame(x = cells_roi$x, y = cells_roi$y,
                       gene_roi[, genes_keep, drop = FALSE], check.names = FALSE)
final_df[1:3, 1:min(6, ncol(final_df))]
```

We analyze one gene in detail. The input to DenMark is a data frame with the
columns `x`, `y` and the gene's counts.

```{r gene, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Cell-level expression of the selected gene."}
# [Code Block 2.4] Select the gene of interest
stopifnot(gene_choice %in% names(final_df))
df_gene <- final_df[, c("x", "y", gene_choice)]

ggplot(df_gene, aes(x, y, color = .data[[gene_choice]])) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "gray92", high = "red", trans = "sqrt") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("x (", unit_label, ")"), y = paste0("y (", unit_label, ")"),
       color = gene_choice) +
  theme_classic()
```

**Gridding.** `buildgridpp()` assigns every cell to exactly one grid cell and
returns the counts $Y(g)$ and the summed expression $M(g)$, both as vectors and
as matrices. With `boundary = tissue`, it also returns the area of every grid
cell inside the tissue. `grid_pts_centroid()` returns the grid geometry.
DenMark keeps the grid cells inside the tissue, centers them at the origin so
that the ROI becomes $[-L_1, L_1]\times[-L_2, L_2]$, and uses the grid
centroids as the HSGP coordinates. This is done inside `DenMark()`, so you no
longer need to compute $L_1$ and $L_2$ yourself.

```{r grid}
# [Code Block 2.5] Grid the data
grid_res <- buildgridpp(grid_size = grid_size, dataset = df_gene, boundary = tissue)
names(grid_res)
# grid_res[[1]]: N x 2 matrix of cell counts Y and expression M
# grid_res[[2]]: matrix of cell counts;  grid_res[[3]]: matrix of expression
head(grid_res$grid[grid_res$grid$type != "exterior", ])

geom <- grid_pts_centroid(grid_size = grid_size, dataset = df_gene,
                          bbox = grid_res$bbox)
c(full_grid_area = geom$grid_area, n_grids = geom$N)

# the Stan input that DenMark() builds internally, useful for checks
prep <- denmark_prepare(df_gene, gene = gene_choice, grid_size = grid_size,
                        basis = basis_choice, boundfactor = boundary_choice,
                        boundary = tissue)
c(n_grids_in_tissue = prep$stan_data$n, interior = prep$info$n_interior,
  boundary = prep$info$n_boundary, L1 = prep$info$L1, L2 = prep$info$L2,
  HSGP_basis_total = prep$stan_data$mstar)
summary(exp(prep$stan_data$log_grid_area))   # clipped areas of the grid cells
```

```{r grid-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Gridded cell counts and gene expression in the grid cells inside the tissue."}
# [Code Block 2.6] Visualize the gridded data
plot_denmark_grid(grid_res, xlab = unit_label, ylab = unit_label)
```

# 3. Single-gene analysis: quantify the density-expression association

## 3.1 Fit the full and the simplified DenMark models

`DenMark()` grids the data, builds the HSGP inputs, compiles the Stan model
once per session, sets valid initial values and samples. `model = "M2"`
fits the full model and `model = "M1"` the simplified model. Passing
`boundary = tissue` restricts the fit to the tissue. The fits are
saved with `denmark_save()` so they can be reloaded without refitting.

```{r fit}
# [Code Block 3.1] Run the full and simplified DenMark versions
fit_or_load <- function(file, ...) {
  if (!params$refit && file.exists(file)) return(denmark_load(file))
  fit <- do.call(DenMark, c(list(...), mcmc))
  denmark_save(fit, file)
  fit
}
tag <- paste(gene_choice, grid_size, basis_choice, params$iter_sampling, "alpha",
             sep = "_")

denmark_full <- fit_or_load(file.path(fit_dir, paste0("M2_", tag, ".rds")),
                            dataset = df_gene, gene = gene_choice, model = "M2",
                            grid_size = grid_size, basis = basis_choice,
                            boundfactor = boundary_choice, boundary = tissue,
                            quiet = TRUE)

denmark_simple <- fit_or_load(file.path(fit_dir, paste0("M1_", tag, ".rds")),
                              dataset = df_gene, gene = gene_choice, model = "M1",
                              grid_size = grid_size, basis = basis_choice,
                              boundfactor = boundary_choice, boundary = tissue,
                              quiet = TRUE)
denmark_full
```

## 3.2 Posterior summaries

For the full model: $\beta_0, \beta_1$ are the intercepts of the cell density
and gene expression intensities, `ell[1]`, `ell[2]` the length-scales of the
two latent fields, `Astar[2,1]` $=\rho$ the density-expression correlation,
and `sigma[1]`, `sigma[2]` the standard deviations of the two fields. R-hat
close to 1 and large effective sample sizes (ESS) indicate convergence.

```{r summary}
# [Code Block 3.2] Posterior summaries
cols <- c("variable", "mean", "sd", "q2.5", "q50", "q97.5", "rhat",
          "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
show_table(denmark_summary(denmark_full)[, cols], caption = "Full DenMark (M2).")
show_table(denmark_summary(denmark_simple)[, cols],
           caption = "Simplified DenMark (M1): a11 and a22 are the field SDs.")
```

```{r rho, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "Posterior distribution of the density-expression correlation."}
# [Code Block 3.3] Posterior of rho
draws_full <- denmark_draws(denmark_full)   # rho, a11, a21, a22, ell1, ell2, ...
rho_ci <- quantile(draws_full$rho, c(0.025, 0.975))

ggplot(draws_full, aes(rho)) +
  geom_density(fill = "gray80") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rho_ci, color = "firebrick", linetype = 3) +
  xlim(-1, 1) +
  labs(x = expression(rho), y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_classic()
```

The posterior mean of $\rho$ for `r gene_choice` is
**`r sprintf("%.3f", mean(draws_full$rho))`** with 95% credible interval
(`r sprintf("%.3f", rho_ci[1])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", rho_ci[2])`).

## 3.3 Model comparison and diagnostics

```{r waic}
# [Code Block 3.4] WAIC comparison: lower WAIC is better
cmp <- denmark_compare(full_M2 = denmark_full, simplified_M1 = denmark_simple)
show_table(cmp[, c("model", "waic", "waic_se", "p_waic", "elpd_diff", "se_diff")],
           digits = 2)

# sampler diagnostics and running time
diag_row <- function(f) with(f$diagnostics, data.frame(
  divergences = num_divergent, treedepth_hits = num_max_treedepth,
  max_rhat = max_rhat, min_ess_bulk = min_ess_bulk, minutes = f$time))
show_table(cbind(model = c("M2", "M1"),
                 rbind(diag_row(denmark_full), diag_row(denmark_simple))), digits = 3)
```

`elpd_diff` is the difference in expected log predictive density relative to
the best model, and `se_diff` is its standard error. A difference of several
standard errors in favor of M2 supports a density-expression dependence.

The HSGP approximation can be checked against the rule of thumb of
Riutort-Mayol et al. (2023). If the posterior length-scale is shorter than
`ell_min`, increase `basis`. If `boundary_ok` is `FALSE`, increase
`boundfactor`. The rule is conservative, so treat it as guidance.

```{r hsgp}
# [Code Block 3.5] HSGP adequacy check
show_table(denmark_check_hsgp(denmark_full, warn = FALSE))
```

## 3.4 Latent field decomposition

`denmark_fields()` returns, for every grid cell, the posterior means of the
log cell density $\beta_0 + a_{11}w_1$ and the log expression per cell
$\beta_1 + a_{21}w_1 + a_{22}w_2$, decomposed into the density field
$a_{11}w_1$, the density-shared expression component $a_{21}w_1$, and the
expression-specific component $a_{22}w_2$.

```{r fields, fig.height = 5.8, fig.cap = "Latent field decomposition (posterior means). Top: cell density; bottom: gene expression."}
# [Code Block 3.6] Latent field decomposition
fields_full <- denmark_fields(denmark_full)
head(fields_full[, c("grid_index", "Y", "M", "eta1", "a11w1", "eta2", "a21w1", "a22w2")], 3)
plot_denmark_fields(denmark_full, fields = fields_full, xlab = unit_label, ylab = unit_label)
```

## 3.5 Spatial correlation functions and ranges

The density field decays as $r_1(d) = \mathcal{M}(d;\ell_1)$. The expression
field decays as
$r_2(d) = \{a_{21}^2\mathcal{M}(d;\ell_1) + a_{22}^2\mathcal{M}(d;\ell_2)\}/(a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2)$,
where $\mathcal{M}$ is the Matérn-3/2 correlation. The practical range is the
distance at which the correlation drops to 0.05. It is computed for every
posterior draw.

```{r decay, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Posterior spatial correlation functions (mean and 95% band)."}
# [Code Block 3.7] Spatial correlation decay
decay_full <- denmark_decay(denmark_full, threshold = 0.05)
plot_denmark_decay(denmark_full, decay = decay_full,
                   xlab = paste0("Distance (", unit_label, ")"))
show_table(decay_full$ranges, caption = "Practical ranges (distance where correlation = 0.05).")
```

The estimated range is `r sprintf("%.2f", decay_full$ranges$mean[1])`
`r unit_label` for cell density and
`r sprintf("%.2f", decay_full$ranges$mean[2])` `r unit_label` for the
expression of `r gene_choice`.

# 4. DCG discovery: identify the density-correlated genes

`denmark_scan()` fits the full model to each candidate gene and classifies it
from the 95% credible interval of $\rho$:

* **PCG**, a positively density-correlated gene: the interval lies above 0;
* **NCG**, a negatively density-correlated gene: the interval lies below 0;
* **not DCG**: the interval contains 0.

Here we scan a few genes. For the whole panel, pass all filtered genes, set
`save_dir` so that each gene is saved as it finishes and an interrupted scan
resumes where it stopped, and consider running the genes in parallel on a cluster.
`fit_simple = TRUE` also fits M1 and reports the WAIC difference per gene.

```{r scan, eval = params$run_scan}
# [Code Block 4.1] Scan candidate genes
scan_genes <- intersect(scan_genes, names(final_df))
dcg <- do.call(denmark_scan,
               c(list(data = final_df, genes = scan_genes,
                      grid_size = grid_size, basis = basis_choice,
                      boundfactor = boundary_choice, boundary = tissue,
                      verbose = FALSE,
                      save_dir = file.path(fit_dir, paste0("scan_", tag))),
                 mcmc))
show_table(setNames(dcg[, c("gene", "rho_mean", "rho_lower", "rho_upper",
                            "class", "max_rhat")],
                    c("gene", "rho", "2.5%", "97.5%", "class", "R-hat")))
```

```{r scan-plot, eval = params$run_scan, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "Density-expression correlation across genes (posterior mean and 95% credible interval)."}
# [Code Block 4.2] Forest plot of rho
plot_denmark_scan(dcg)
```

```{r scan-all, eval = FALSE}
# [Code Block 4.3] Full-panel scan
dcg_all <- denmark_scan(final_df, genes = genes_keep, grid_size = grid_size,
                        basis = basis_choice, boundfactor = boundary_choice,
                        boundary = tissue, save_dir = "denmark_scan_all")
table(dcg_all$class)
subset(dcg_all, class == "PCG")$gene
subset(dcg_all, class == "NCG")$gene
```

# 5. The same workflow in Python

`denmark.py` provides the same functions for Python, using **cmdstanpy** and
the same Stan files. Given the same data, it builds identical Stan inputs and
returns the same summaries. The example below runs on the simulated data; the
commented lines show how to load the Xenium files instead.

```{python, eval = FALSE}
# [Code Block 5.1] Python
# install once: pip install cmdstanpy pandas scipy matplotlib shapely
#               python -m cmdstanpy.install_cmdstan
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "DenMark")
import pandas as pd
import denmark as dm

# simulated section: analyzed cell type plus other cells in an irregular tissue
sim = dm.simulate(rho={"geneA": 0.6, "geneB": 0.0, "geneC": -0.6},
                  width=6, height=4, n_cells=5000, seed=1,
                  tissue="irregular", n_other=4000, celltype="Invasive_Tumor")
cells = sim[["x", "y", "celltype"]]
df = sim.loc[sim["celltype"] == "Invasive_Tumor", ["x", "y", "geneA", "geneB", "geneC"]]
gene, genes_to_scan = "geneA", ["geneA", "geneB", "geneC"]

# optional: Xenium data instead
# cells = pd.read_csv("cell_spatial.csv")
# genes = pd.read_csv("cell_by_gene_expression.csv")
# cells[["x", "y"]] /= 1000                        # micrometers -> mm
# sel = cells["celltype"] == "Invasive_Tumor"
# expr = genes.loc[sel].iloc[:, 1:]
# keep = dm.filter_genes(expr)                     # QC filter
# df = pd.concat([cells.loc[sel, ["x", "y"]], expr[keep]], axis=1)
# gene, genes_to_scan = "CDH1", ["CDH1", "ERBB2", "EPCAM", "KRT8"]

# tissue boundary from ALL cells, then the grid restricted to the tissue
tissue = dm.alpha_shape(cells["x"], cells["y"])
grid = dm.buildgridpp(10, df[["x", "y", gene]], boundary=tissue)
dm.plot_boundary(cells, tissue, grid=grid,
                 highlight=cells["celltype"] == "Invasive_Tumor")

full   = dm.DenMark(df[["x", "y", gene]], gene=gene, model="M2", grid_size=10,
                    basis=25, boundfactor=1.5, boundary=tissue)
simple = dm.DenMark(df[["x", "y", gene]], gene=gene, model="M1", grid_size=10,
                    basis=25, boundfactor=1.5, boundary=tissue)
print(full)                                        # rho, WAIC, diagnostics
print(dm.compare_models(full_M2=full, simplified_M1=simple))
fields = full.fields(); decay = full.decay()
dm.plot_fields(full); dm.plot_decay(full)

dcg = dm.scan_genes(df, genes=genes_to_scan, grid_size=10, basis=25,
                    boundary=tissue, save_dir="scan_py")
dm.plot_scan(dcg)
```
